### Comparing Results

We compare logistic regression, the pruned decision tree, and the SVM on the
same 184 test patients (102 with heart disease, 82 without), using the same
0.50 classification threshold. The baseline of always predicting "disease" is
55.4% accurate, so every model has to beat that.

| Model | Accuracy | Sensitivity | Specificity | AUC |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Baseline (always "disease") | 0.554 | 1.000 | 0.000 | 0.500 |
| Logistic Regression | 0.875 | 0.882 | 0.866 | 0.930 |
| Decision Tree | 0.821 | 0.814 | 0.829 | 0.898 |
| SVM (linear) | 0.886 | 0.892 | 0.878 | 0.932 |
| SVM (radial) | 0.886 | 0.892 | 0.878 | 0.932 |

```{r comp-roc, fig.height=4.5, fig.width=6}
roc_all <- list(log_roc, tree_roc, res_linear$roc)
names(roc_all) <- c(
  sprintf("Logistic Regression (AUC = %.3f)", auc(log_roc)),
  sprintf("Decision Tree (AUC = %.3f)",       auc(tree_roc)),
  sprintf("SVM (AUC = %.3f)",                  auc(res_linear$roc))
)

ggroc(roc_all, legacy.axes = TRUE, linewidth = 1) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey") +
  labs(title = "ROC Curves for All Models (Test Set)",
       x = "1 - Specificity", y = "Sensitivity", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = c(0.65, 0.2))
```

**Predictive performance.** All three models are far more accurate than the
baseline. The SVM is the strongest on every metric (88.6% accuracy, AUC 0.932),
logistic regression is very close behind (87.5%, AUC 0.930), and the decision
tree is clearly last (82.1%, AUC 0.898). The gap between the SVM and logistic
regression is one patient: the SVM makes 21 mistakes on the test set and
logistic regression makes 23. That difference is not meaningful. A DeLong test
on the AUCs gives p = 0.74 for logistic regression versus the linear SVM, so we
cannot say the SVM is better. The tree's AUC is lower than logistic
regression's by 0.032, which is suggestive but not significant at the 0.05
level (p = 0.084).

**Linear vs. flexible models.** The radial SVM, which can draw curved
boundaries, performed identically to the linear SVM on the test set. Cross-
validation also preferred the linear kernel (12.9% error versus 13.2%) and
pushed the radial kernel's gamma to the smallest value we tried, which makes
its boundary nearly straight. The tree can also capture nonlinear effects and
interactions, yet it did worst. Together this suggests the relationship between
the clinical predictors and heart disease is close to linear, so extra
flexibility mostly adds variance rather than accuracy.

**Errors that matter.** Missing a patient who has heart disease is the costlier
mistake, so sensitivity matters most here. The SVM misses 11 of 102 patients
with heart disease (sensitivity 0.892), logistic regression misses 12 (0.882),
and the tree misses 19 (0.814). The tree is the only model that gives a false
negative in roughly one of every five disease cases.

**Interpretability.** The models differ more in what they tell us than in how
well they predict:

- *Logistic regression* gives an odds ratio for each predictor. Male sex
  (odds ratio 6.2), a flat ST slope compared to a downward slope (3.8),
  fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dl (2.9), exercise-induced angina (2.0), and
  each additional unit of ST depression (1.5) all raise the odds of heart
  disease. Chest pain types other than asymptomatic (ATA, NAP, TA) have odds
  ratios around 0.2, and an upward ST slope lowers the odds (0.36). A zero
  cholesterol reading, which we treated as missing, was also strongly
  associated with disease (odds ratio 5.2). Age, resting blood pressure,
  cholesterol, maximum heart rate, and resting ECG were not significant once the
  other predictors were included.
- *The decision tree* gives simple rules a clinician could follow. It splits
  first on ST slope, then on chest pain type, ST depression, and maximum heart
  rate. For example, patients with a flat or downward ST slope and asymptomatic
  chest pain were classified as having heart disease about 90% of the time. The
  tree agrees with logistic regression on which variables matter, but a single
  tree is less stable and has to give the same predicted probability to every
  patient in a leaf, which limits its AUC.
- *The SVM* predicts well but gives no coefficients or rules, so it tells us how
  well heart disease can be predicted without telling us which variables drive
  the prediction.

**Overall.** The SVM and logistic regression are effectively tied for the best
predictive performance, and the tree is somewhat worse. Because logistic
regression matches the SVM while also explaining *why* each patient is
classified the way they are, it offers the best balance of performance and
interpretability, and it is the model we would choose.
